summary: Karen L. Brock works in Japanology, history and archaeology, and Buddhist studies. She earned her Ph.D. from Princeton University and held assistant professorships in Japanese art at Washington University in St. Louis (attested 1988) and the University of Michigan (attested 1990).

Karen McCarthy Brown (1942–2015) was a religious studies scholar. She studied at Smith College, Union Theological Seminary, and Temple University, and was a professor of anthropology at Drew University (~1976–2009) alongside posts at Temple and other institutions.
Karen Nelson Villanueva is a scholar in religious studies. She earned her PhD at the California Institute of Integral Studies and studied under traditional teacher Geshe Ngawang Dakpa.
Karen Nero has held academic posts at the University of Canterbury and the University of Otago, and she taught Sally McAra.

Karen O'Brien-Kop works in Indology, Buddhist studies, and religious studies. After completing her PhD at SOAS University of London, she held posts at SOAS, the University of Roehampton (attested 2020), and King's College London (attested 2026).

Karin Meyers specializes in Buddhist studies and philosophy. She studied under Jay L. Garfield and served at Kathmandu University as an assistant professor and director of the MA program in Buddhist studies at the Centre for Buddhist Studies at Rangjung Yeshe Institute.

Karin Preisendanz (born 1958) is an Indologist and philosopher. She studied at the University of Hamburg (Dr. phil., Habilitation), and held posts at the Free University of Berlin (1987–1990), University of British Columbia (1990–1993), and University of Vienna (1999).

Karl Ammer (1911–1970) was an Indologist and linguist. He studied at the University of Vienna (~1930–1935) and served as Director of the Institute of Indology at Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg (~1954–1970).

Karl Benedikt Hase (1780–1864) was a scholar of linguistics and history. He studied at Jena and Helmstedt, and later held long-term posts at the Bibliothèque nationale de France (~1805–1864), École nationale des langues orientales vivantes, and the Faculty of Arts of Paris.

Karl Brugmann (1849–1919) was a linguist and Indologist. He studied under Georg Curtius at Leipzig and Halle, later serving as an Ordinarius at the University of Freiburg (1884) and Professor of Indo-European Linguistics at Leipzig University (1887–1919).

Karl Brunnhölzl specializes in Tibetology and Buddhist studies. He received his training under traditional teachers including Khenpo Tsultrim Gyamtso Rinpoche, Tenga Rinpoche, Dzogchen Ponlop Rinpoche, 10th Sangye Nyenpa Rinpoche, Ringu Tulku, and Lama Thubten.

Karl Debreczeny is a scholar of Tibetology and history/archaeology. He completed his PhD at the University of Chicago, where he studied under Hung Wu and Jenny Purtle, and served as a curator at the Rubin Museum of Art (attested 2008).

Karl Eduard Zachariae von Lingenthal (1812–1894) was a history and archaeology scholar. He studied at the universities of Leipzig, Berlin, and Heidelberg, and later held a post at Heidelberg University from ~1836 to 1845.
Karl Eugen Neumann (1865–1915) was a scholar of Buddhist studies and Indology. He studied at Leipzig University (~1887–1888) and pursued his doctorate under Richard Pischel (~1889–1891).
Karl Felix Halm (1809–1882) was a scholar in linguistics, history, and archaeology. He held posts at the University of Munich and the Bavarian State Library from ~1856 to 1882.

Karl Ferdinand Johansson (1860–1926) was an Indologist and linguist. He studied at Uppsala University, where he later served as University Professor of Sanskrit and the Comparative Philology of the Indo-European Languages (~1893–1925).

Karl Florenz (1865–1939) worked in Japanology, Indology, and linguistics, studying at Leipzig and Berlin under Ernst Windisch and others. He taught at the University of Tokyo (1889–1917), Hamburgisches Kolonialinstitut (~1914–1935), and the University of Hamburg (~1919–1935).

Karl Friedrich Geldner (1852–1929) was an Indologist and Iranian studies scholar. He studied at Leipzig and Tübingen under Rudolf von Roth, later holding posts at Tübingen, Halle, Humboldt University of Berlin, and the University of Marburg (1907–1921).
Karl G. Heider (born 1935) studied at Williams College (~1952–1953), Harvard College (~1953–1956), and Harvard University (~1958–1966).

Karl Harrington Potter (1927–2022) specialized in Indology and philosophy. He studied at UC Berkeley and Harvard University under Daniel H. H. Ingalls, and held professorships at the University of Minnesota (attested 1969) and the University of Washington (attested 1987–1999).
